chunks: And as for the report which Al-Husayn ibn Sa'id narrated from Safwan ibn Yahya, from Al-'Ala', from Muhammad ibn Muslim, from one of the Imams (peace be upon them both), who said:

He was asked about the Mu'tamatti' (one performing Hajj al-Tamattu'), how much is sufficient for him? He said: 'A sheep.' And I asked him about the Mu'tamatti' who is a slave, so he said: 'Upon him is like what is upon the free person, either a sacrificial animal (Udhiyah) or fasting.'

This report can be understood in two ways: One is that he was a slave and then was freed before one of the two stations (of Hajj) passed for him, for the sacrificial animal (Hady) becomes obligatory upon him because his Hajj sufficed for him, and the state remains as we described, and we have clarified that previously. The other way is that the master, if he did not command his slave to fast until the last day of departure (Yawm al-Nafar), then it becomes obligatory upon the master to slaughter on his behalf, and fasting will not suffice for him.

key_terms.الْمُتَمَتِّعِ: One performing Hajj al-Tamattu' (pilgrimage with Umrah and Hajj combined)

ai.seo_question: What is the ruling for a slave performing Hajj al-Tamattu' regarding the sacrificial offering?
ai.summary: This narration from *Tahdhib al-Ahkam* clarifies the fidya (expiation) for a slave performing Hajj al-Tamattu', establishing that the obligation mirrors that of a free person—either a sacrifice or fasting. Al-Tusi elucidates two juristic interpretations: either the slave remains liable for his own expiation if freed before the stations pass, or the master bears the cost of the sacrifice if he fails to command the slave to fast until the final departure, highlighting the master's supervisory role in the slave's religious duties.
